To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

rice roots grown under conditions of root flooding accumulate malic acid and VLCFAs, and the expressions of genes encoding plastid enzymes involved in malic acid metabolism are up-regulated under these conditions.
the metabolic profiles and gene expressions in rice roots grown in stagnant conditions are characterized by the accumulations of both malic acid and VLCFAs.

the formation of barrier to radial oxygen losses in rice roots grown in stagnant conditions is associated with malic acid accumulation and the up-regulation of genes encoding plastid localized enzymes that convert malic acid into acetyl CoA, which is used to synthesize very long chain fatty acid.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the biochemical changes in the roots of rice plants grown under stagnant conditions and the possible physiological roles of these changes.
the biochemical and molecular characterization of roots of rice plants that form a barrier to ROL.
a new aspect of the metabolic regulation of suberization in rice roots.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the accumulation of malic acid in rice roots grown in stagnant conditions is a consequence of the up-regulation of the plastid-localized genes encoding the enzymes involved in the conversion of malic acid to AcCoA, and that this malic acid accumulation is a key step in the formation of the barrier to ROL in rice roots.
malic acid accumulation is a key step in the biosynthesis and formation of a suberin barrier in rice roots.

malic acid accumulates in the root cells of rice plants growing in stagnant water and this accumulation is associated with the biosynthesis of very long chain fatty acid (VLCFA) in the outer cell layer of the root and that VLCFA is used in the biosynthesisis of the suberin polymer, which forms a barrier to ROL.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
malic acid accumulation and VLCFA accumulation are two biochemical features of rice roots grown under submergence stress, and the former is closely related to the biosynthesis of VLCFAs.

the formation of the barrier to ROL in rice roots involves the up-regulation of plastid-localized metabolic pathways in the outer cell layer, which is the site where the barrier is located, to supply substrates for the biosynthesis fatty acids.
malic acid and VLCFAs accumulate in rice roots grown in stagnant conditions to provide a substrate and a building block for the biosynthesis and deposition of suberin, respectively.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the accumulation of malic acid in roots grown under stagnant deoxy-genated conditions is an important step in suberin biosynthesis, and this may also be true for other plants.
malic acid accumulation is a key feature of roots forming a barrier, and that this accumulation is a prerequisite for the biosynthesis and incorporation of VLCFAs into suberin.

suberin biosynthesis in rice roots is dependent on malic acid accumulation, which is induced in the outer root cell layers in response to stagnant conditions, suggesting that the formation of a barrier in roots to ROL is a highly coordinated metabolic process.
